one_liner: Dependency-free no_std Rust crate with Wyrand, Xorshift and SplitMix-style PRNGs; README shows about 2x fastrand and 6x rand's ChaCha12.
what_it_does: Defines a small Rand trait (next_u16/u32/u64/u128/usize, next_bool(Probability), next_lim and next_range for unsigned integers and Duration) plus a Seeded trait, and ships three 64-bit-state generators; StdRand is an alias for Wyrand. Companion crates add clock seeding and a thread-local generator (tinyrand-std) and a closure-driven Mock for tests (tinyrand-alloc). It has its own trait rather than rand_core's RngCore, so it is not a drop-in for rand or fastrand call sites.
how_it_is_fast: Each generator is a single u64 with an #[inline(always)] next_u64; the default Wyrand step is a Weyl increment (0xA0761D6478BD642F), one 64x64-to-128-bit multiply and an xor fold. Bounded integers up to 64 bits use Lemire's multiply-shift method with a rarely taken rejection loop (credited in the README); ranges wider than 64 bits fall back to modulo with rejection. There is no buffering, reseeding or cryptographic work, which is where most of the gap to rand's ChaCha12 thread_rng comes from.
when_to_use: no_std or bare-metal Rust (microcontrollers, kernels) that needs fast non-cryptographic u64s or bounded integers without a heap.
Unit tests that must force random branches: the tinyrand-alloc Mock lets a test script next_u128, next_bool and next_lim results and count invocations.
Jitter, randomized backoff, games and simulations where a 64-bit Weyl-sequence generator (Wyrand) is good enough and you want one tiny dependency-free crate.
Per-thread generators in std code via tinyrand-std's thread_rand, seeded from the system clock.
when_not_to_use: Anything security-sensitive: the README says none of the generators is cryptographically secure and points to rand for a CSPRNG.
You need floats or distributions: the Rand trait has no f64 method and no normal, exponential or shuffle helpers (issue #2 asks how to make floats); signed-integer ranges are not implemented either.
Code built on the rand ecosystem: it does not implement rand_core::RngCore, so rand's distributions, SliceRandom and seeding helpers cannot use it directly.
Long or parallel simulations with Xorshift: its state recurrence has period 2^48-1, not 2^64-1 (see gotchas); use Wyrand or a larger-state generator.
C++ projects: Rust only, with no C ABI.

integration.dependencies: none (tinyrand); optional companion crates tinyrand-std and tinyrand-alloc
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; lib.rs uses inline format arguments (Rust 1.58+, inferred); no rust-version declared; CI pinned to Rust 1.66.0
integration.platforms: any (no_std, no architecture-specific code; next_usize is defined for 16/32/64/128-bit pointer widths; CI tests x86-64 and i686-unknown-linux-gnu via cross)
integration.thread_safety: Generators are plain u64 structs mutated through &mut self with no internal synchronization; give each thread its own instance or use tinyrand-std's thread-local thread_rand.

gotchas: Default::default() uses a constant seed (0 for Wyrand, 1 for Xorshift and SplitMix), so every run repeats the same sequence unless you seed it (README warns); issue #1 (2023) reports the README examples always returning 0 and was closed with no visible reply.

Xorshift is not textbook xorshift64: it saves the state after the <<13 and >>7 steps and applies <<17 only to the output. A GF(2) analysis run this session gives a characteristic polynomial with factors of degree 8, 8 and 48, so ordinary seeds cycle after 2^48-1 outputs (about 2.8e14, roughly 4 days at the README's 6.7 GB/s) instead of 2^64-1, and 65,535 nonzero seeds (for example 0x1e250d05b6eea0) cycle after 51 or 255 steps; no seed in 1..2^20 hits those short cycles.

SplitMix is not Steele/Lea/Flood SplitMix64: it has no Weyl increment and iterates x -> (x ^ x>>32) * 0xff51afd7ed558ccd mod 2^64 (a bijection with 0 as a fixed point, which seed() avoids), so its period depends on the seed and is not guaranteed; constants and shifts differ from the splitmix64.c reference (0x9e3779b97f4a7c15 increment, shifts 30/27/31).
next_u16 and next_u32 return the low bits of next_u64, and next_lim, next_range and Probability::new panic (assert!) on a zero limit, an empty range or p outside [0, 1]; there is no fallible API.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tinyrand over simd-rand when you draw one value at a time, need no_std or bounded integers and mocks; pick simd-rand for bulk u64 fills, where its portable Xoshiro256+X8 path reports 8.52 Gelem/s and the AVX-512 path is faster still. For C or C++ code the same Wyrand idea is available in lemire/testingRNG, which also benchmarks it against lehmer64 and PCG.
verified_claims_summary: The README table lists bandwidth in GB/s: rand ChaCha12 (thread_rng) 2.4, tinyrand SplitMix 6.5, Xorshift 6.7, fastrand Wyrand 7.5 and tinyrand Wyrand 14.6, with no CPU, toolchain, flags, date or formula for GB/s. The public criterion bench (cri_rand.rs; criterion 0.3.6, rand 0.8.5, fastrand 1.8.0) times single calls, but its fastrand row times a bounded u64(0..u64::MAX) call while the tinyrand rows time raw next_u64, and the rand row is a reseeding CSPRNG. The only same-algorithm comparison, Wyrand 14.6 versus 7.5 GB/s (about 1.9x, derived from page data), is therefore partly a call-shape difference rather than generator speed.
status_note: Abandoned since late 2022 (crate 0.5.0 published 2022-09-12, about 92k total downloads per crates.io, CI pinned to Rust 1.66.0), but MIT, dependency-free and small enough to vendor; prefer Wyrand and avoid the Xorshift and SplitMix variants.
